opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly, for us it comes down to how research actually happens. In AI research, especially now, things move incredibly fast. If you put the leaders in a separate office down the hall, information flows through layers, and by the time a problem reaches them, or a decision comes back down, the moment has often passed.

When everyone sits together, a lot of the important exchanges are informal. Someone is stuck on an experiment, the loss curve looks strange, and they can just turn around and say, "Hey, have you seen this before?" Those five-minute conversations often turn out to matter more than a formal weekly meeting. As someone who still likes to do hands-on research myself, I want to be close to that. I want to see the actual results, the actual bugs, not just a polished slide deck a week later.

There's also a cultural reason. Research works best when ideas are judged on their merit, not on who proposed them. If the manager sits in a corner office, there's an implicit message that the hierarchy matters more than the idea. Sitting together flattens that a bit. A junior researcher can challenge me directly, and frankly, they're often right, because they're the ones closest to the data and the code.

And for me personally, it keeps me honest. It's very easy, as you become more senior, to drift into abstraction, to start talking about "strategy" without really knowing what's working on the ground. Sitting with the team forces me to stay connected to the real technical problems, which is where I think good research direction actually comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says that sitting together prevents information from flowing through layers and enables quick informal exchanges, clearly linking shared seating to better communication.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the simple answer is that I don't think of myself as a "boss" in the traditional sense. In research, the person who has the best idea on a given day might be a first-year engineer, not the person with the title. If I'm sitting in a separate office behind a door, I'm not going to hear that idea. I'll hear it three weeks later in a slide deck, after it's already been polished and maybe after the interesting part has been smoothed out.

Sitting together changes the information flow. People can turn around and ask a question in thirty seconds instead of scheduling a meeting. I overhear debugging sessions, I see when someone is stuck, and I can jump in before a problem turns into a week of wasted effort. And it goes the other way too: people see me struggling with my own experiments, writing code, getting results that don't make sense. That matters. It shows that research is messy for everyone, and it takes away a lot of the fear of looking stupid in front of the manager.

There's also a cultural part. In many places, especially where I grew up, hierarchy is very strong, and people won't challenge a senior person directly. I think that's really bad for research. Good ideas get killed because nobody wants to say the leader is wrong. Physical proximity is a small but concrete signal that we're all working on the same problem, and the problem doesn't care about your title.

Of course it has costs. It's noisier, and I have less uninterrupted time. But for me, the trade-off is clearly worth it. The job of a research lead is mostly to keep the team pointed in the right direction and to remove obstacles quickly, and you can't do that well if you're isolated from what's actually happening at the desks.

r001.rationale: The response says sitting together improves information flow and lets people ask questions immediately, clearly connecting shared seating with easier communication.

astra-6.text: The idea is to make communication easier. When managers and employees sit together, people can ask questions, share ideas, and discuss problems as they come up, instead of waiting for a formal meeting. It also helps managers understand the day-to-day work. There’s less distance between making a decision and hearing from the people who have to carry it out.

r001.rationale: It says sitting managers and employees together makes communication easier, allowing questions, ideas, and problems to be discussed as they arise.

sol-6.1.text: The idea is to reduce the barrier to communication. If a manager sits in a separate office, people may feel they need to make an appointment or have a fully developed idea before bringing it up. When everyone sits together, you can ask a quick question, discuss a problem, or share an idea while it’s still taking shape. That’s especially useful in research, where nobody has all the answers. You want people to feel comfortable challenging an idea, regardless of who proposed it.

r001.rationale: The response says that sitting together reduces barriers to communication and makes it easier to ask questions, discuss problems, and share ideas.
